children: The Japanese government is considering deploying over 100 satellites for the nation's satellite constellation, a surveillance system in which multiple small satellites are used together to track and detect targets, according to government and ruling party sources.

The move is aimed at improving Japan's ability to stage counterattacks, meant to neutralize adversaries with long-range missiles. By improving surveillance, which is essential for identifying targets, the government hopes to strengthen deterrence. There are plans to include the measure in three key security documents, which are expected to be revised by the end of the year, according to the sources.

The Defense Ministry aims to improve its ability to identify moving targets, such as naval vessels and transporter erector launchers (TELs), and to make continuous tracking more accurate by significantly increasing the number of satellites that will be used in the system. Under the current plan, the constellation is supposed to include several dozen units.

The information collected through the system is also expected to be used for maritime surveillance, with the aim of strengthening the defense system along Japan's Pacific coast, where there are few early warning and control radars, according to the sources.

China and North Korea have large numbers of TELs, making it difficult to determine missile launch sites beforehand. The government plans to rely on satellite intelligence from the U.S. military to detect moving targets for the time being, but building its own satellite network is a high priority.

The current plan calls for establishing a surveillance network consisting of several dozen satellites by the end of fiscal 2027. The plan extends to the end of fiscal 2030, and the ministry allocated 283.2 billion yen for this purpose in the initial budget for fiscal 2025.

The ministry is arranging to more than double the relevant budget as it now expects the surveillance system to have more than 100 satellites under the next phase of the plan for fiscal 2031 onward, according to the sources.

As in the current plan, a private finance initiative would be used to bolster the constellation, with domestic companies owning and operating satellites. The ministry intends to retain priority access to satellite imagery. If capacity allows, companies would be allowed to sell imagery to other firms and other entities, according to the sources.
The ministry is looking to create "a virtuous cycle between defense and the economy" by energizing the space industry, a senior ministry official said.

A stronger satellite network is key for enhancing the effectiveness of standoff missiles, which can be launched at a distance from an enemy. In March, the Self-Defense Forces deployed Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missiles, which have a range of over 1,000 kilometers, in Kumamoto Prefecture. And in late August, the Chokai — an Aegis-equipped destroyer capable of firing a U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missile, which has a range of more than 1,600 kilometers — returned to its home port in Nagasaki Prefecture after modification work.

The sources said that apart from this surveillance system, the ministry is also aiming to create an observation network to detect and track hypersonic glide vehicles, which are currently being developed by China and Russia.
